{{Short description|Interface between solid and liquid phases}}
In [[thermal equilibrium]], each [[phase (matter)|phase]] (i.e. [[liquid]], [[solid]] etc.) of physical [[matter]] comes to an end at a transitional point, or spatial [[interface (matter)|interface]], called a '''phase boundary''', due to the [[immiscibility]] of the matter with the matter on the other side of the boundary.  This immiscibility is due to at least one difference between the two substances' corresponding physical properties. The behavior of phase boundaries has been a developing subject of interest and an active interdisciplinary research field, called [[interface and colloid science|interface science]], for almost two centuries, due partly to phase boundaries naturally arising in many physical processes, such as the [[capillarity effect]], the growth of [[grain boundary|grain boundaries]], the physics of [[binary alloy]]s, and the formation of [[snow flake]]s. 

One of the oldest problems in the area dates back to Lamé and Clapeyron<ref>[[Gabriel Lamé|G. Lamé]], [[Benoît Paul Émile Clapeyron|B. P. Clapeyron]], Memoire sur la solidification par refroiddissement d'un globe solide, Ann. Chem. Physics, 47, 250–256  (1831).</ref> who studied the freezing of the ground. Their goal was to determine the thickness of solid crust generated by the cooling of a liquid at constant [[temperature]] filling the [[Half-space (geometry)|half-space]]. In 1889, Stefan, while working on the freezing of the ground developed these ideas further and formulated the two-phase model which came to be known as the [[Stefan problem | Stefan Problem]].<ref>[[Josef Stefan|J. Stefan]], Über einige Probleme der Theorie der Warmeleitung, S.-B Wien Akad. Mat. Natur, 98, 173–484, (1889).</ref>

The proof for the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the [[Stefan problem]] was developed in many stages. Proving the general existence and uniqueness of the solutions in the case of <math>d=3</math> was solved by [[Shoshana Kamin]].
